title: Introduction to Medical Virology — Lecture I
summary: Viruses are obligate intracellular submicroscopic infectious agents that replicate only inside living cells and can infect animal, plant, bacterial, and protozoal cells.

The term virus comes from Latin and means poison or toxic fluid; the discovery history begins with Dmitri Ivanovsky's 1892 tobacco-mosaic-virus filtration experiment and Martinus Beijerinck's 1898 interpretation.
Three hypotheses have been proposed for virus origin: regressive, escape/progressive, and co-evolution/virus-first; none has been clearly confirmed to date.
Viruses are classified according to size, structure, genome, physical properties, chemical properties, and target tissue.
Viral particles contain a core and capsid, with an envelope present in some viruses and matrix protein in enveloped viruses; capsid plus nucleic-acid core forms the nucleocapsid.
The viral genome contains either DNA or RNA, not both, and may be single- or double-stranded, linear or circular, and segmented or non-segmented.
The capsid protects viral nucleic acid, participates in delivery into host cells through attachment proteins, determines antigenic characteristics, and determines viral symmetry.
Major viral symmetry patterns are icosahedral, helical, and complex. Viral envelopes are lipoprotein structures whose lipid portion is derived from host membranes.

Physical and chemical stability varies with heat, cold, dryness, ultraviolet radiation, ether/chloroform, glycerol, formaldehyde, chlorine, and iodine. Target-cell specificity is described by viral tropism.

Viral replication proceeds through adsorption, penetration, uncoating, synthesis of viral macromolecules, assembly, and release; viral particles may be complete, defective, pseudoviruses, or coreless, while subviral agents include prions and viroids.

keyTerms.definition: An agent that requires a living host cell for replication and cannot thrive and reproduce outside the living cell.
The term used by Martinus Beijerinck for the filtered infectious agent; infectious, living, fluid.
The hypothesis that viruses began as small pre-virus cells that lost metabolic and reproductive abilities and became dependent on host-cell pathways.
The capsid together with the viral nucleic-acid core.
The ability of a virus to specifically infect a particular cell, tissue, or host that supports its replication.
The phase during viral macromolecule synthesis when no viral particles can be detected inside the infected host cell.
A premature virus with an incomplete genome that can require a helper virus for replication.
A small proteinaceous infectious particle made of misfolded protein without detected nucleic acid.

flashcards.front: Why are viruses called obligate intracellular agents?
flashcards.back: They replicate only inside living cells because they cannot thrive and reproduce outside the living cell.

flashcards.front: Who first discovered the infectious agent later identified as tobacco mosaic virus?
flashcards.back: Dmitri Ivanovsky in 1892, after filtration of infected tobacco-plant extracts.

flashcards.front: What did Beijerinck call the new infectious agent?
What are the three hypotheses for virus origin?

flashcards.back: The capsid plus the nucleic-acid core.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between +sense and -sense RNA?
flashcards.back: +sense RNA acts as mRNA and is directly translated; -sense RNA acts as a template for mRNA synthesis first.

flashcards.front: What are the three viral symmetry types?
What are the two main methods of viral release?

questions.question: Which statement best defines viruses according to the lecture?
options: They are free-living microorganisms that reproduce on ordinary culture media
They are obligate intracellular submicroscopic infectious agents that replicate only inside living cells
They are protein-only particles that infect plants exclusively
They are bacteria that have lost their cell walls
questions.explanation: The lecture defines viruses as obligate intracellular submicroscopic infectious agents that replicate only inside living cells.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Viruses require living cells for replication.
Correct. This matches the lecture definition.
Incorrect. Prions are proteinaceous subviral agents, while viruses infect many types of cells.
Incorrect. Viruses are not bacteria lacking cell walls.
questions.hint: Focus on the requirement for a living cell.

questions.question: Which hypothesis for the origin of viruses suggests they began as pre-virus cells (like Chlamydia) that infected larger cells, subsequently losing metabolic and reproductive abilities to become inert, dependent particles?
questions.explanation: The regressive hypothesis proposes that viruses originated from small pre-virus cells (similar to Chlamydia) that infected larger cells and gradually lost their metabolic and reproductive abilities, becoming dependent on host cellular pathways.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Co-evolution proposes viruses evolved alongside or before host cells.
Incorrect. The escape hypothesis involves mobile genetic elements leaving their cellular environment.
Correct. This accurately describes the regressive hypothesis using the Chlamydia example.
Incorrect. The progressive hypothesis involves MGEs gaining capsid genes.
questions.hint: Think about the theory involving reduction or loss of functions in pre-virus cells like Chlamydia.

questions.question: Why did Ivanovsky's filtration experiment suggest that the tobacco-mosaic infectious agent was not an ordinary bacterium?
options: The agent grew rapidly on ordinary culture media
The infectious filtrate passed through a Chamberland filter
The agent was easily seen by the light microscope
The agent became noninfectious after filtration
questions.explanation: Ivanovsky found that the filtrate remained infectious after passage through a Chamberland filter that normally retains bacteria and fungi.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Growth on ordinary culture media was not the key observation.
Correct. Continued infectivity after filtration was the key finding.
Incorrect. The lecture does not identify that as the discovery basis.
Incorrect. The filtrate remained infectious.
questions.hint: Remember what the Chamberland filter normally retains.

questions.question: According to the escape (progressive) hypothesis, viruses originated from mobile genetic elements (MGEs) like retrotransposons that gained capsid and enzyme genes. Which of the following is a classic example of a virus that evolved via this progressive mechanism?
questions.explanation: The progressive (escape) hypothesis suggests viruses evolved from mobile genetic elements such as retrotransposons, which subsequently gained capsid protein and viral enzyme genes. Retroviruses are a classic example of this evolutionary pathway.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Pithovirus is a giant virus, not an example of the progressive hypothesis.
Correct. Retroviruses are cited as an example of the progressive (escape) hypothesis.
Incorrect. Parvoviruses are small DNA viruses, not the classic example for this hypothesis.
Incorrect. Chlamydia is used as an example for the regressive hypothesis, not the progressive one.
questions.hint: Recall which virus is linked to mobile genetic elements like retrotransposons.

questions.question: Who repeated Ivanovsky's experiment in 1898 and used the term 'contagium vivum fluidum'?
questions.explanation: Martinus Beijerinck repeated the experiment in 1898 and described the filtered infectious agent as contagium vivum fluidum.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Ivanovsky performed the earlier 1892 experiment.
Incorrect. Prusiner coined the term prion in 1982.
Correct. Beijerinck made the 1898 interpretation.
Incorrect. Pasteur is not identified here as the scientist who named the agent.
questions.hint: Think of the 1898 scientist.

questions.question: Which hypothesis proposes that viruses have evolved before their host cell or coevolved along with their host cell over time?
questions.explanation: The co-evolution (virus-first) hypothesis proposes that viruses have been evolved before their host cell or coevolved along with their host cell.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The regressive hypothesis involves pre-virus cells losing functions.
Incorrect. The escape hypothesis involves MGEs.
Incorrect. The progressive hypothesis is another name for the escape hypothesis.
Correct. This matches the definition of the co-evolution hypothesis.
questions.hint: Look for the hypothesis name that directly mentions evolving alongside or before the host.

questions.question: Which hypothesis proposes that viruses arose from small cells that lost metabolic and reproductive abilities?
questions.explanation: The regressive hypothesis proposes that pre-virus cells lost metabolic and reproductive abilities and became dependent on host-cell pathways.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Escape involves mobile genetic elements leaving their original cellular environment.
Incorrect. Co-evolution proposes evolution before or alongside the host cell.
Correct. This is the regressive/reduction hypothesis.
Incorrect. Capsid mispackaging is related to pseudovirus formation.
questions.hint: Look for the theory involving reduction or loss of functions.

questions.question: What is the maximum magnification power of a Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) as mentioned in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that the Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) has a magnification power of up to 50,000,000x.
optionExplanations: Correct. The TEM has a maximum magnification of up to 50,000,000x.
Incorrect. This is not the stated maximum for TEM.
Incorrect. This is lower than the stated maximum.
Incorrect. This is lower than the stated maximum.
questions.hint: Remember the maximum magnification number given for TEM.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a criterion for classification of viruses?
questions.explanation: The listed criteria are size, structure, genome, physical properties, chemical properties, and target tissue.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Genome is listed.
Incorrect. Target tissue is listed.
Incorrect. Physical properties are listed.
Correct. Antibiotic susceptibility is not listed.
questions.hint: Review the six classification criteria.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a virus with its size category?
questions.explanation: According to the lecture, Poxviridae is classified as a large size virus measuring 250-400 nm. Parvoviridae and Picornaviridae are small (<20-30 nm), Herpesviridae is medium (150-200 nm), and Pithovirus sibericum is a very large (Giant) virus measuring 1500 nm.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Pithovirus sibericum is a very large (Giant) virus (1500 nm).
Incorrect. Herpesviridae is a medium size virus (150-200 nm).
Correct. Poxviridae is classified as large (250-400 nm).
Incorrect. Picornaviridae is a small size virus (20-30 nm).
questions.hint: Match the virus family to the correct size category as defined in the lecture.

questions.question: According to the lecture, viruses generally range in size from approximately:
questions.explanation: The lecture states that viruses range from about 20 to 400 nm; giant viruses can exceed 400 nm.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is below the stated range.
Correct. This is the general range given.
Incorrect. This is not the stated general range.
Incorrect. The lecture gives the unit as nanometers.
questions.hint: Remember the unit as well as the endpoints.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the visualization of viruses is correct?
options: All viruses are visible under a light microscope
Some large viruses and all giruses are seen by the light microscope
Only small viruses (<30 nm) are visible under a light microscope
Viruses are never visible under a light microscope
questions.explanation: The lecture notes that some large viruses and all giruses (giant viruses) are visible under the light microscope.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Most viruses are too small to be seen with a light microscope.
Correct. Large viruses and all giruses can be seen by light microscopy.
Incorrect. Small viruses are not visible under a light microscope.
Incorrect. Large and giant viruses are exceptions to this rule.
questions.hint: Consider the exceptions mentioned regarding large and giant viruses.

questions.question: Which method determines viral size indirectly using a collodion membrane of graded porosity?
questions.explanation: Ultrafiltration uses a collodion membrane with graded pore sizes to estimate viral size.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Electron microscopy directly determines size.
Incorrect. Ultracentrifugation uses sedimentation rate.
Correct. This is the collodion membrane method.
Incorrect. Light microscopy is not the method described.
questions.hint: Think about the membrane-filter method.

questions.question: How long can Herpesvirus survive on hard dry surfaces according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lecture states that while rotavirus cannot survive longer than 8 hours on hard dry surfaces, herpesvirus can survive up to 8 weeks on hard dry surfaces.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is the survival time for rotavirus.
Incorrect. The lecture specifies up to 8 weeks.
Incorrect. The lecture specifies up to 8 weeks.
Correct. Herpesvirus can survive up to 8 weeks on hard dry surfaces.
questions.hint: Compare the dry surface survival times of rotavirus and herpesvirus.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the resistance of Adenovirus and Poliovirus to ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI)?
options: Poliovirus is highly resistant, while Adenovirus is less resistant
Adenovirus is highly resistant, while Poliovirus is less resistant
questions.explanation: According to the lecture, adenovirus is highly resistant to inactivation by UV radiation, while poliovirus is less resistant to inactivation by UV radiation.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Poliovirus is less resistant, not highly resistant.
Correct. Adenovirus is highly resistant, while poliovirus is less resistant.
Incorrect. Their resistance levels differ according to the lecture.
Incorrect. Adenovirus is noted for its high resistance.
questions.hint: Remember which virus was highlighted as highly resistant and which was less resistant.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the viral genome?
options: It contains both DNA and RNA in every virus
It contains either DNA or RNA, not both
questions.explanation: The viral genome contains either DNA or RNA, not both. Either type may be single- or double-stranded.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The lecture explicitly says DNA or RNA, not both.
Correct. This is the central statement about viral genome composition.
Incorrect. DNA viral genomes can be single- or double-stranded.
Incorrect. RNA genomes can also be double-stranded.
questions.hint: The key phrase is DNA OR RNA.

questions.question: Which non-structural viral protein is responsible for controlling the metabolic functions of the host cell?
questions.explanation: Non-structural (functional) proteins include regulatory proteins that control the metabolic functions of the host cell, as outlined in the lecture.
optionExplanations: Correct. Regulatory proteins are non-structural proteins that control host cell metabolic functions.
Incorrect. Structural capsid proteins form the physical viral particle, not regulatory functions.
Incorrect. Reverse transcriptase is an enzyme carried in the virion, not primarily a host metabolic regulator.
Incorrect. Envelope glycoproteins are structural components.
questions.hint: Which non-structural protein type specifically controls host metabolic functions?

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a non-structural viral protein that functions as an enzyme involved in the replication of the viral genome?
questions.explanation: Non-structural (functional) proteins include enzymes involved in the replication of the viral genome, such as RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in negative-sense RNA viruses.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Capsid proteins are structural proteins.
Incorrect. Peplomers are envelope glycoprotein spikes (structural).
Correct. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is a non-structural enzyme involved in viral genome replication.
Incorrect. Matrix proteins are structural components of enveloped viruses.
questions.hint: Which of these options is a non-structural enzyme specifically involved in viral genome replication?

questions.question: A positive-sense RNA viral genome is one that:
options: Must first be converted to DNA before translation
Acts as mRNA and is directly translated to protein
Cannot serve as a template for protein synthesis
questions.explanation: Positive-sense RNA acts as mRNA and is directly translated into protein.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is not the lecture's definition of positive-sense RNA.
Correct. Positive-sense RNA functions directly as mRNA.
Incorrect. It is directly translated.
Incorrect. Sense refers to coding orientation, not strand number.
questions.hint: Positive-sense RNA behaves like mRNA.

questions.question: Which non-structural viral protein directly affects the viral release from the infected cell?
questions.explanation: The lecture lists non-structural proteins that affect the viral release from the infected cell as a specific functional category.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Reverse transcriptase is involved in genome replication.
Incorrect. Capsid proteins are structural.
Incorrect. Regulatory proteins control host metabolic functions.
Correct. Proteins that affect viral release are a specific category of non-structural proteins.
questions.hint: Which protein category is explicitly linked to the release process?

questions.question: Which is a function of the viral capsid?
options: Protecting viral nucleic acid from nucleases
Supplying all ATP for viral replication
questions.explanation: Protection of the viral nucleic acid from nucleases is one of the four capsid functions listed in the lecture.
optionExplanations: Correct. The lecture explicitly lists protection from nucleases.
Incorrect. ATP is supplied by the host cell.
Incorrect. Host ribosomes remain necessary for protein synthesis.
Incorrect. The capsid is not a universal anti-mutation mechanism.
questions.hint: Think of the capsid's protective role.

questions.question: Which of the following statements correctly differentiates early from late viral transcription and translation?
options: Early processes synthesize polymerases and regulatory proteins, while late processes synthesize structural proteins and proteins required for viral release
Early processes synthesize structural proteins and proteins required for viral release, while late processes synthesize polymerases and regulatory proteins
Early processes synthesize viral genome replication, while late processes synthesize host DNA
Early processes synthesize envelope lipids, while late processes synthesize capsid proteins
questions.explanation: Early transcription and translation are required for the synthesis of early viral proteins such as polymerases, regulatory proteins, and viral-specific antigens. Late transcription and translation are required for replication of the viral genome and synthesis of late viral proteins such as structural proteins, viral enzymes, and proteins required for viral release.
optionExplanations: Correct. This accurately describes the products of early and late transcription/translation phases.
Incorrect. The order is reversed; polymerases are early, structural proteins are late.
Incorrect. Late processes include viral genome replication, not host DNA synthesis.
Incorrect. Envelope lipids are host-derived, and capsid proteins are late structural proteins.
questions.hint: Think about what needs to be made first (enzymes for replication) versus what is made later (structural components).

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes icosahedral viral symmetry?
options: Capsomers and genome are twisted into a spiral tube provides a flexible structure
It results from twenty equilateral triangles and provides a highly rigid structure
It has no defined capsomer arrangement
It occurs only in enveloped DNA viruses
questions.explanation: The lecture describes icosahedral symmetry as an arrangement of twenty equilateral triangles that provides a highly rigid structure.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. A spiral tube describes helical symmetry.
Correct. This matches the lecture's description.
Incorrect. Complex symmetry is the one without icosahedral or helical orientation.
Incorrect. The lecture does not restrict icosahedral symmetry this way.
questions.hint: Think of the 20 triangular faces of an icosahedron.

questions.question: Which pairing is correctly matched?
options: Helical symmetry — capsomers and genome twist together
Complex symmetry — twenty equilateral triangular faces
Icosahedral symmetry — capsomers and genome form a spiral tube
questions.explanation: The lecture defines helical symmetry as capsomers and genome twisted together and lists Orthomyxoviridae as an example.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Twenty triangles describe icosahedral symmetry.
Incorrect. The spiral tube describes helical symmetry.
Incorrect. Complex symmetry is exemplified by poxvirus and bacteriophage.
questions.hint: Match the geometry to the description.

questions.question: Which of the following viruses is associated with Pharyngitis?
questions.explanation: Adenovirus is associated with Pharyngitis.
questions.hint: Think of the respiratory and throat infections.

questions.question: Which statement about heat sensitivity is correct according to the lecture?
options: Enveloped viruses are generally heat sensitive
All viruses are immediately destroyed by cold storage
Non-enveloped viruses are always heat sensitive
Most viruses are most unstable at -70 °C
questions.explanation: The lecture states that enveloped viruses are heat sensitive while non-enveloped viruses are heat resistant. It also notes that most viruses are stable at -40 to -70 °C.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the lecture's heat classification.
Incorrect. Most viruses are stable at -40 to -70 °C.
Incorrect. The lecture gives the opposite comparison.
Incorrect. The lecture says most viruses are stable in that cold range.
questions.hint: Compare enveloped with non-enveloped viruses under heat.

questions.question: Which virus is the causative agent of Gingivostomatitis?
questions.explanation: Herpes simplex type 1 is associated with Gingivostomatitis.
questions.hint: Think of the herpes virus types.

questions.question: What is the main function of the viral genome?
questions.explanation: The viral genome codes for virus-specific macromolecules.
optionExplanations: Correct. The genome carries the information for virus-specific macromolecules.
Incorrect. Capsid assembly is a downstream process.
Incorrect. Viruses do not produce ATP.
Incorrect. Viruses do not directly perform host-cell division.
questions.hint: The genome holds the genetic information.

questions.question: Which virus is associated with Cardiovascular infections?
questions.explanation: Coxsackie B virus is associated with Cardiovascular infections.
questions.hint: Think of the virus associated with heart infections.

questions.question: What is the capsid?
options: Lipid membrane obtained from the host cell wall
questions.explanation: The capsid is an impermeable protein shell around viral nucleic acid.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes the envelope.
Correct. The capsid is the protein shell.
Incorrect. The capsid is made of protein, not RNA.
Incorrect. The capsid is viral, not a host receptor.
questions.hint: It is the protective protein shell.

questions.question: Which of the following viruses cause Hepatitis?
options: Types A, B, C, D, E
Types A, B, C, D, E
questions.explanation: Hepatitis viruses include types A, B, C, D, and E.
questions.hint: How many types of hepatitis viruses are there?

questions.question: What are capsomers?
questions.explanation: Capsomers are protein subunits composed of polypeptide molecules.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They are not lipids.
Incorrect. They are viral structural units.
Correct. Capsomers are protein subunits.
Incorrect. They are structural proteins, not the genome.
questions.hint: They are the building blocks of the capsid.

questions.question: Which virus is associated with Pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Coxsackie B virus is associated with Pancreatitis.
questions.hint: Think of the virus that also causes heart infections.

questions.question: What are capsomers in structural virology?
options: Morphological protein subunits that assemble to form the protective viral capsid around the nucleic acid.
Glycoprotein spikes projecting from the viral envelope that mediate host receptor binding.
Hydrophobic lipid bilayer domains derived from the host cell membrane during viral budding.
Internal non-structural proteins that stabilize the viral genome within the nucleocapsid matrix.
questions.explanation: Capsomers are the fundamental structural/morphological protein units (composed of one or more polypeptide chains) that self-assemble into a symmetrical outer shell called the capsid, which encloses and protects the viral genetic material.
optionExplanations: Correct. Capsomers are proteinaceous structural subunits that aggregate to constitute the viral capsid.
Incorrect. Glycoprotein spikes projecting from the envelope are termed peplomers, which mediate target receptor attachment.
Incorrect. Lipid bilayer domains belong to the viral envelope acquired from the host host membrane, not capsomers.
Incorrect. Non-structural or matrix proteins serve functional or scaffold roles inside the virion rather than forming the structural capsomeric shell.
questions.hint: Distinguish between the structural protein shell units (capsid) and outer envelope surface spikes (peplomers).

questions.question: What is the genome type of Parvovirus?
questions.explanation: Parvovirus has a single-stranded DNA (linear) genome.
questions.hint: It is a small DNA virus.

questions.question: What does viral symmetry describe in structural virology?
options: The spatial arrangement and geometric pattern formed by capsomers in the viral capsid.
The precise stoichiometry and copy number of the enclosed viral genome.
The thermodynamic stability threshold of the lipid envelope under varying temperatures.
The degree of evolutionary conservation between host cell receptor binding sites.
questions.explanation: Viral symmetry refers to the geometric arrangement of protein subunits (capsomers) that assemble to form the protective capsid shell surrounding the viral genome, classically categorized into helical, icosahedral (cubic), or complex symmetries.
optionExplanations: Correct. Viral symmetry denotes the spatial architecture and geometric organization (e.g., icosahedral vs. helical) of the capsid proteins.
Incorrect. Genome stoichiometry and nucleic acid length relate to genomic organization, not structural capsid symmetry.
Incorrect. Environmental stability and temperature thresholds describe viral physical resistance, not spatial structural symmetry.
Incorrect. Evolutionary conservation of receptor binding domains involves sequence identity and host tropism, unrelated to capsid geometric symmetry.
questions.hint: Think about how capsomers repeat spatially in 3D to form geometric shapes like icosahedrons or helices.

questions.question: What is the genome type of Herpesvirus?
questions.explanation: Herpesvirus has a double-stranded DNA (linear) genome.
questions.hint: It is a large DNA virus.

questions.question: Which set contains all three types of viral symmetry described in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The three types of viral symmetry are icosahedral, helical, and complex.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. These are not the terms used.
Correct. These are the three types described.
Incorrect. These are not the three types.
Incorrect. These are not the three types.
questions.hint: Remember the three geometric arrangements.

questions.question: What is the genome type of M13?
questions.explanation: M13 has a single-stranded DNA (circular) genome.
questions.hint: It is a filamentous phage.

questions.question: How many equilateral triangles are involved in the icosahedral arrangement described in the lecture?
questions.explanation: The icosahedral arrangement involves twenty equilateral triangles.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. There are twenty.
Incorrect. There are twenty.
Correct. Twenty equilateral triangles form an icosahedron.
Incorrect. There are twenty.
questions.hint: Think of a 20-sided die.

questions.question: What is the genome type of Baculovirus?
questions.explanation: Baculovirus has a double-stranded DNA (circular) genome.
questions.hint: It is an insect virus with a circular genome.

questions.question: In the icosahedral symmetry described in the lecture, what are the protein subunits at the angles of each triangular capsomer called?
questions.explanation: The protein subunits at the angles of each triangular capsomer are called pentamers.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They are pentamers.
Incorrect. Peplomers are envelope spikes.
Incorrect. They are pentamers.
Correct. Pentamers form the vertices of the icosahedron.
questions.hint: Think of the 5-sided structure at the vertices.

questions.question: What is the genome type of TMV?
questions.explanation: TMV (Tobacco Mosaic Virus) has a single-stranded RNA (linear) genome.
questions.hint: It is a classic plant RNA virus.

questions.question: How are the capsomers and viral genome arranged in helical symmetry?
options: They are twisted together to form a spiral tube
They are completely separated from each other
They are located only inside the nucleus
They are absent from RNA viruses
questions.explanation: In helical symmetry, the capsomers and viral genome are twisted together to form a spiral tube.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture description.
Incorrect. They are twisted together.
Incorrect. They are in the cytoplasm or virion.
Incorrect. RNA viruses can have helical symmetry.
questions.hint: Think of a spiral tube structure.

questions.question: What is the genome type of Reovirus?
questions.explanation: Reovirus has a double-stranded RNA (linear) genome.
questions.hint: It is a respiratory enteric orphan virus.

questions.question: Which virus was given as an example of complex viral symmetry?
questions.explanation: Poxvirus is given as an example of complex viral symmetry.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Picornavirus has icosahedral symmetry.
Correct. Poxvirus is the classic example of complex symmetry.
Incorrect. Herpesvirus has icosahedral symmetry.
Incorrect. Orthomyxovirus has helical symmetry.
questions.hint: Which virus is known for its complex, brick-like shape?

questions.question: What is the genome type of Hepatitis D virus?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis D virus has a single-stranded RNA (circular) genome.
questions.hint: It is a defective RNA virus.

questions.question: What is the primary cellular origin of the lipid bilayer in an enveloped virus?
options: Host cell membranes incorporated during viral budding or exocytosis.
De novo lipid biosynthesis encoded by non-structural viral enzymes.
Proteolytic cleavage of capsomeric protein complexes within the capsid matrix.
Polymerization of host nuclear DNA components during virion assembly.
questions.explanation: Enveloped viruses acquire their lipid bilayer directly from host cell membranes (such as the plasma membrane, endoplasmic reticulum, or Golgi apparatus) during the process of budding or exocytosis, while viral envelope glycoproteins are inserted prior to release.
optionExplanations: Correct. The lipid bilayer component of the viral envelope is host-derived, captured as the virus buds through host cellular membranes.
Incorrect. Viruses lack the machinery for de novo lipid synthesis and rely entirely on hijacking host cell lipid membranes.
Incorrect. Capsomers are proteinaceous structures that form the capsid, not lipid precursors.
Incorrect. Host cell DNA is a nucleic acid polymer and cannot synthesize or constitute membrane lipids.
questions.hint: Recall how enveloped virions acquire their outer membrane when exiting the host cell through budding.

questions.question: What are the protein spikes projecting from the viral envelope also called?
questions.explanation: Protein spikes projecting from the viral envelope are called peplomers.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Capsomers form the capsid.
Incorrect. Matrix proteins are inside the envelope.
Incorrect. Nucleotides are nucleic acid building blocks.
Correct. Peplomers are the envelope spikes.
questions.hint: They are the glycoprotein spikes on the outside.

questions.question: Which function of the viral envelope is directly related to binding to specific receptors on a host cell?
questions.explanation: The viral envelope's ability to bind to specific receptors determines viral tropism.
optionExplanations: Correct. Binding to specific receptors determines which cells the virus can infect (tropism).
Incorrect. ATP is produced by the host cell.
Incorrect. Genome transcription occurs after entry.
Incorrect. Capsid digestion occurs during uncoating.
questions.hint: Think about what determines which cells a virus can infect.

questions.question: Which of the following is another function of the viral envelope?
options: Evasion of the host immune system
questions.explanation: A function of the viral envelope is to help the virus evade the host immune system.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Genome replication occurs inside the host cell.
Correct. The envelope helps evade the host immune system.
Incorrect. ATP synthesis is a host cell function.
Incorrect. Ribosome formation is a host cell function.
questions.hint: How does the envelope protect the virus from antibodies?

questions.question: Which set contains possible sources of viral envelopes inside the host cell?
options: Plasma membrane, nuclear membrane, Golgi apparatus membrane, and endoplasmic reticulum
questions.explanation: Viral envelopes can be derived from the plasma membrane, nuclear membrane, Golgi apparatus membrane, and endoplasmic reticulum.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Mitochondria are not typically used.
Incorrect. Multiple sources are possible.
Correct. These are the sources listed in the lecture.
Incorrect. The nucleus is not a membrane source.
questions.hint: Which organelles have membranes that can be hijacked?

questions.question: Which set encompasses the primary cellular membrane sources from which enveloped viruses can derive their lipid envelope during maturation and exit?
options: Plasma membrane, nuclear membrane, Golgi apparatus, and endoplasmic reticulum.
Outer mitochondrial membrane, peroxisomal matrix, and lysosomal lumen.
Plasma membrane exclusively, as budding cannot occur across internal organellar membranes.
Ribosomal subunit membranes, nucleolar matrix, and centrosomes.
questions.correctAnswer: Plasma membrane, nuclear membrane, Golgi apparatus, and endoplasmic reticulum.
questions.explanation: Enveloped viruses acquire their lipid bilayer by budding through various host cellular membrane compartments depending on the virus family: Herpesviruses utilize the inner nuclear membrane, Flaviviruses and Coronaviruses bud into the Endoplasmic Reticulum-Golgi Intermediate Compartment (ERGIC), and Retroviruses or Influenza viruses bud predominantly from the plasma membrane.
optionExplanations: Correct. Enveloped viruses can utilize a diverse array of host endomembrane systems (ER, Golgi, nuclear envelope) as well as the outer plasma membrane for envelope acquisition.
Incorrect. Mitochondria, peroxisomes, and lysosomes are not standard functional sites for viral envelope budding during virion assembly.
Incorrect. While many viruses bud at the plasma membrane, numerous families (e.g., Herpesviridae, Coronaviridae) routinely acquire their envelopes from internal organelle membranes.
Incorrect. Ribosomes, nucleoli, and centrosomes are non-membranous cellular structures or organelles lacking lipid bilayers, making envelope derivation impossible.
questions.hint: Consider both cell-surface egress (plasma membrane) and intracellular assembly routes involving the endomembrane network (ER, Golgi, nuclear envelope).

questions.question: Most viruses are stable at approximately which temperature range?
questions.explanation: Most viruses are stable at -40 to -70 °C.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the stable range for most viruses.
Incorrect. This is not the stated range.
Incorrect. This is a high temperature.
Incorrect. This is a very high temperature.
questions.hint: Think of standard cold storage temperatures.

questions.question: Which virus was described in the lecture as unable to survive longer than 8 hours on hard dry surfaces?
questions.explanation: Rotavirus cannot survive longer than 8 hours on hard dry surfaces.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Herpesvirus can survive up to 8 weeks.
Correct. Rotavirus is the virus mentioned with an 8-hour limit.
Incorrect. Poxvirus was not mentioned for this.
Incorrect. HIV was not mentioned for this.
questions.hint: Which virus is sensitive to dryness and survives less than a day?

questions.question: Which genome types are less susceptible to ultraviolet germicidal irradiation (UVGI) than ssDNA and ssRNA viruses?
questions.explanation: dsDNA and dsRNA viruses are less susceptible to UVGI than ssDNA and ssRNA viruses.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. ssRNA is more susceptible.
Incorrect. These are the more susceptible types.
Correct. dsDNA and dsRNA are less susceptible.
Incorrect. ssDNA is more susceptible.
questions.hint: Double-stranded genomes are more resistant to UV damage.

questions.question: Which statement correctly matches a chemical agent with viral sensitivity?
options: Enveloped viruses are sensitive to ether and chloroform
Glycerol destroys viruses and is used as a virucide
Viruses are resistant to formaldehyde, chlorine, and iodine
Non-enveloped viruses are more ether sensitive than enveloped viruses
questions.explanation: The lecture states that enveloped viruses are sensitive to ether and chloroform. Viruses are glycerol resistant, while formaldehyde, chlorine, and iodine are listed as inactivating agents.
optionExplanations: Correct. Ether and chloroform are listed as inactivating agents for enveloped viruses.
Incorrect. Viruses are glycerol resistant.
Incorrect. The lecture says they are sensitive to these agents.
Incorrect. Enveloped viruses are the ether-sensitive group.
questions.hint: Ether and chloroform point to the envelope.

questions.question: Which of the following primary determinants governs cell and tissue tropism during viral infection?
options: The presence and distribution of specific host cell surface receptors and essential cellular transcription factors.
The baseline metabolic rate and systemic core temperature of the host organism during incubation.
The physical stoichiometry and total molecular weight of the capsomeric protein subunits.
The post-translational lipidation state of host extracellular matrix fibronectin.
questions.explanation: Viral tropism—the specificity of a virus for infecting particular cell types, tissues, or host species—is primarily determined by susceptibility (expression of complementary surface receptors/co-receptors for entry) and permissiveness (availability of intracellular factors such as transcription factors required for viral replication).
optionExplanations: Correct. Host cell receptor expression and intracellular transcriptional machinery directly dictate viral susceptibility and tissue tropism.
Incorrect. Host core temperature may influence systemic immunity or replication kinetics, but it does not define the cell-surface specificity of viral tropism.
Incorrect. Capsomer copy number and total capsid weight define virion architecture, not host tissue selectivity.
Incorrect. Matrix lipidation is an extracellular host trait unrelated to the specific receptor-ligand interactions that drive viral tropism.
questions.hint: Consider both cellular susceptibility (surface receptor recognition) and permissiveness (intracellular machinery for replication).

questions.question: Which sequence correctly lists the six general steps of viral replication in the order given in the lecture?
options: Assembly → adsorption → release → penetration → uncoating → synthesis
Adsorption → penetration → uncoating → synthesis of viral macromolecules → assembly → release
Penetration → adsorption → synthesis → release → assembly → uncoating
Adsorption → assembly → penetration → uncoating → release → synthesis
questions.explanation: The six sequential steps are adsorption, penetration, uncoating, synthesis of viral macromolecules, assembly, and release.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The lecture places adsorption first and assembly later.
Correct. This is the exact order given.
Incorrect. The order of adsorption and later events is wrong.
Incorrect. Assembly does not occur immediately after adsorption.
questions.hint: Start with attachment and end with release.

questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes a defective virus from a coreless virus?
options: A defective virus has an incomplete genome; a coreless virus has no nucleic-acid core
A defective virus has no capsid; a coreless virus has a complete genome
Both are complete mature viruses with complete genomes
A coreless virus can replicate with a helper virus
questions.explanation: A defective virus contains an incomplete genome and may replicate with a helper virus, whereas a coreless virus contains no nucleic-acid core and cannot infect or replicate.
optionExplanations: Correct. This matches the lecture definitions.
Incorrect. Defective viruses still have capsids.
Incorrect. Neither description matches the lecture.
Incorrect. Coreless viruses lack nucleic acid and cannot replicate even with a helper virus.
questions.hint: Compare what is inside the particle.

questions.question: Which chemical agents are viruses sensitive to according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Viruses are sensitive to formaldehyde, chlorine, and iodine.
optionExplanations: Correct. These are the agents listed.
Incorrect. Viruses are glycerol resistant.
Incorrect. Ether affects enveloped viruses, but these are the general agents.
Incorrect. Viruses are resistant to glycerol.
questions.hint: Which agents are used as disinfectants?

questions.question: Why is glycerol added to viral suspensions?
questions.explanation: Glycerol is added to viral suspensions to prevent bacterial contamination, as viruses are glycerol resistant.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Glycerol does not destroy the genome.
Correct. Glycerol prevents bacterial contamination.
Incorrect. Glycerol does not affect tropism.
Incorrect. Glycerol does not promote replication.
questions.hint: What is glycerol used for in a lab setting?

questions.question: What is viral tropism?
options: The ability of a virus to survive drying
The ability of a virus to divide in the host cell using host cell machinery
The ability of a virus to specifically infect a particular cell or tissue
The ability of a virus to resist ultraviolet radiation
questions.explanation: Viral tropism is the ability of a virus to specifically infect a particular cell, tissue, or host that supports its replication.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes resistance to drying.
Incorrect. This describes capsid assembly.
Correct. This is the definition of viral tropism.
Incorrect. This describes UV resistance.
questions.hint: It defines the specific cells a virus can infect.

questions.question: Which set of biological determinants directly governs both viral susceptibility and cellular permissiveness to define viral tropism?
options: Host cell wall thickness and ribosomal RNA sedimentation coefficients.
Viral envelope lipid composition and genomic segment length.
Capsid icosahedral symmetry and environmental incubation temperature.
Specific host cell surface receptors and essential intracellular transcription factors.
questions.explanation: Viral tropism relies on two key constraints: susceptibility (determined by specific cell-surface receptors and co-receptors that allow entry) and permissiveness (determined by intracellular host factors, such as specific transcription factors, necessary for viral gene expression and replication).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Animal host cells lack cell walls, and ribosomal sedimentation coefficients are general translational properties unrelated to viral tropism.
Incorrect. Envelope lipids and segment length affect biophysical stability and genome structure, but do not determine cell-type-specific tropism.
Incorrect. Capsid symmetry dictates physical geometry, and temperature influences enzymatic kinetics, but neither governs cellular recognition or permissiveness.
Correct. Surface receptors mediate attachment/entry (susceptibility), while intracellular transcription factors enable replication (permissiveness), jointly defining tropism.
questions.hint: Think about the two phases of infection: host cell entry (susceptibility) and intracellular replication (permissiveness).

questions.question: Which of the following virus groupings exemplifies an organ- or tissue-system classification scheme based primarily on viral tropism and clinical pathology?
options: Respiratory viruses, enteric/gastrointestinal viruses, dermatotropic viruses, and neurotropic viruses.
Positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses, double-stranded RNA viruses, and reverse-transcribing DNA viruses.
Enveloped helical viruses, non-enveloped icosahedral viruses, and complex symmetry viruses.
Fastidious viruses, obligate intracellular viruses, and environmental filterable agent viruses.
questions.explanation: Classifying viruses according to target organs or anatomical sites of pathology divides them based on tissue tropism and clinical presentation (e.g., respiratory, enteric/gastrointestinal, neurotropic, dermatotropic, or hepatotropic viruses), in contrast to structural, genomic, or Baltimore classification systems.
optionExplanations: Correct. Grouping by organ system or target site (e.g., neurotropic, dermatotropic, respiratory, enteric) constitutes a pathology- and tropism-based anatomical classification.
Incorrect. Categorizing by positive/negative-sense ssRNA, dsRNA, or reverse transcription follows the Baltimore classification system based on genome replication strategy.
Incorrect. Distinguishing between enveloped/non-enveloped and helical/icosahedral arrangements reflects physical and morphological structural classification.
Incorrect. Terms like obligate intracellular or filterable agents represent historical physiological and microbiological characteristics, not a target-organ system classification.
questions.hint: Distinguish between biological classification based on target tissue/pathology versus structural morphology or genomic replication mechanisms.

questions.question: Why does a virus require the machinery of a host cell for replication?
options: Because viruses contain no genetic material
Because viruses cannot attach to cells
Because viruses are unable to contain proteins
questions.explanation: Viruses are metabolically inert and rely on host cell machinery for replication.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Viruses contain DNA or RNA.
Correct. Viruses are metabolically inert.
Incorrect. Viruses can attach to cells.
Incorrect. Viruses contain proteins.
questions.hint: They lack their own metabolism.

questions.question: Which cellular component provides the protein-synthesizing machinery required for viral replication?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes provide the protein-synthesizing machinery required for viral replication.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Capsids are viral structural proteins.
Incorrect. Peplomers are viral envelope spikes.
Correct. Ribosomes are the host cell's protein factories.
Incorrect. Viral envelopes are lipid membranes.
questions.hint: Which host organelle makes proteins?

questions.question: Which set of low-molecular-weight biological precursors must be supplied by the host cell metabolic machinery to sustain viral protein synthesis and genomic replication?
options: Intact cellular ribosomes and structural histone octamers.
Nucleoside triphosphates, amino acids, and tRNA molecules.
Fatty acyl-CoA esters and complex phospholipid monomers exclusively.
Pre-assembled viral capsomers and functional envelope glycoproteins.
questions.explanation: Because viruses lack independent metabolic pathways and biosynthetic machinery, they depend entirely on host cellular pools of low-molecular-weight building blocks—specifically nucleoside triphosphates (for genome replication) and amino acids charged on host tRNAs (for viral protein translation).
questions.subtopic: Viral Replication and Host Cell Machinery
optionExplanations: Incorrect. While viruses utilize host translational machinery, ribosomes and histones are complex macro-assemblies rather than the fundamental small chemical precursors used as building blocks.
Correct. Nucleoside triphosphates (building blocks for RNA/DNA) and amino acids (building blocks for proteins) are the primary small-molecule precursors provided by the host cell.
Incorrect. While lipid precursors are required by enveloped viruses for membrane synthesis, replication strictly requires nucleotide and amino acid pools for genomic and proteomic synthesis.
Incorrect. Capsomers and glycoproteins are viral-encoded structural end-products of translation and assembly, not low-molecular-weight precursor substrates supplied by the host.
questions.hint: Focus on the fundamental building blocks required by polymerase and ribosomal enzymes to synthesize viral nucleic acids and proteins.

questions.question: How does a virus redirect the host cell to produce viral-specific proteins?
questions.explanation: Viral mRNA is translated by host ribosomes into viral-specific proteins.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Host ribosomes are used, not destroyed.
Correct. Viral mRNA is translated into viral proteins.
Incorrect. ATP is not converted to DNA.
Incorrect. The envelope is not involved in translation.
questions.hint: What molecule carries the genetic message to the ribosome?

questions.question: Viral mRNA is synthesized by transcription of which viral genomes according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Viral mRNA is synthesized by transcription of DNA or negative-sense RNA genomes.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. dsRNA is not the only source.
Incorrect. Positive-sense RNA is directly translated, not transcribed to mRNA.
Correct. DNA and negative-sense RNA are transcribed to mRNA.
Incorrect. Circular DNA is not the only source.
questions.hint: Which genomes need to be transcribed to make mRNA?

questions.question: Which of the following is a structural viral protein?
questions.explanation: Capsid protein is a structural viral protein.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Reverse transcriptase is a non-structural enzyme.
Incorrect. Regulatory proteins are non-structural.
Incorrect. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is a non-structural enzyme.
Correct. Capsid protein is structural.
questions.hint: Which protein forms the physical structure of the virus?

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-structural viral protein?
questions.explanation: Viral enzymes are non-structural viral proteins.
optionExplanations: Correct. Viral enzymes are non-structural.
Incorrect. Capsid protein is structural.
Incorrect. Peplomer is a structural envelope protein.
Incorrect. Envelope lipid is not a protein.
questions.hint: Which of these is a functional protein?

questions.question: Which enzyme is carried as a virion component by retroviruses?
questions.explanation: Retroviruses carry reverse transcriptase as a virion component.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They carry reverse transcriptase.
Correct. Reverse transcriptase is carried by retroviruses.
Incorrect. Peptidase is not the enzyme mentioned.
Incorrect. ATP synthase is not carried by retroviruses.
questions.hint: Which enzyme converts RNA to DNA?

questions.question: Which enzyme is carried by negative-sense RNA viruses as a virion component?
questions.explanation: Negative-sense RNA viruses carry RNA-dependent RNA polymerase as a virion component.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Reverse transcriptase is carried by retroviruses.
Incorrect. DNA ligase is not carried by these viruses.
Correct. RNA-dependent RNA polymerase is carried by negative-sense RNA viruses.
Incorrect. ATP synthase is not carried by these viruses.
questions.hint: Which enzyme is needed to transcribe negative-sense RNA into positive-sense mRNA?

questions.question: Which statement about the number of proteins encoded by viruses is correct?
options: All viruses encode exactly the same number of proteins
Small viruses always encode more proteins than large viruses
The number of proteins is unrelated to genome size
Large viruses can produce many proteins because they have larger genomes
questions.explanation: Large viruses can produce many proteins because they have larger genomes.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The number varies greatly.
Incorrect. Large viruses typically encode more proteins.
Incorrect. Genome size is directly related to the number of proteins.
Correct. Larger genomes allow for more protein-coding capacity.
questions.hint: Think about the relationship between genome size and protein number.

questions.question: What is the correct sequence of the six major steps of viral replication?
options: Adsorption → penetration → uncoating → synthesis → assembly → release
Penetration → adsorption → synthesis → assembly → uncoating → release
Adsorption → synthesis → penetration → assembly → release → uncoating
Uncoating → adsorption → penetration → synthesis → release → assembly
questions.explanation: The correct sequence is adsorption, penetration, uncoating, synthesis, assembly, and release.
optionExplanations: Correct. This is the correct sequence.
Incorrect. Penetration follows adsorption.
Incorrect. Synthesis follows uncoating.
Incorrect. Uncoating follows penetration.
questions.hint: Start with attachment, end with release.

questions.question: What is viral adsorption?
options: adhesion of the protein matrex to capsid shell to form envelopd virus
Recognition and attachment of the virus to the host cell
Separation of the viral genome from the capsid
Formation of new viral particles through budding or cell lysis
questions.explanation: Viral adsorption is the recognition and attachment of the virus to the host cell through viral attachment proteins binding to specific receptors.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is not the adsorption.
Correct. This is the definition of adsorption.
Incorrect. This describes uncoating.
Incorrect. This describes assembly.
questions.hint: It is the first step of infection.

questions.question: Which of the following cellular structures serves as the specific ligand binding partner for Viral Attachment Proteins (VAPs) during the adsorption phase of infection?
options: Intracellular eukaryotic translation initiation factors (eIFs) within host cytosol.
Complementary protein, glycoprotein, or glycolipid cell-surface microdomains on the host plasma membrane.
Host genomic promoter sequences containing canonical TATA-box motifs.
questions.explanation: Viral attachment proteins (VAPs), such as hemagglutinin or envelope glycoproteins, specifically recognize and bind to cell-surface receptors (proteins, glycoproteins, or glycolipids) on the host plasma membrane during the initial attachment phase, which determines host range and cellular tropism.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Translation initiation factors are cytosolic cellular machinery involved in protein synthesis, not surface receptors for viral adsorption.
Correct. VAPs recognize specific surface molecules—including proteins, carbohydrate moieties of glycoproteins, or glycolipids—to mediate attachment.
Incorrect. Host genomic promoter sequences are nuclear nucleic acid structures, inaccessible during initial virion attachment at the cell exterior.
Incorrect. ABC transporters are functional transmembrane pumps and do not serve as general attachment receptors for viral adsorption.
questions.hint: Consider the extracellular surface structures that interact with virion surface proteins prior to entry or membrane fusion.

questions.question: What is the term used for viral penetration by endocytosis?
questions.explanation: Viropexis is the term used for viral penetration by endocytosis.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Tropism is tissue specificity.
Incorrect. Budding is a release mechanism.
Incorrect. Assembly is a later step.
Correct. Viropexis refers to endocytosis.
questions.hint: It is a specific term for endocytic penetration.

questions.question: How do non-enveloped viruses generally enter the host cell?
options: By direct genome injection into the nucleus
questions.explanation: Non-enveloped viruses generally enter the host cell by endocytosis.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Budding is a release mechanism.
Correct. Endocytosis is the primary entry method.
Incorrect. Nuclear membrane fusion is not the general method.
Incorrect. Direct injection is not the general method.
questions.hint: They are taken up in vesicles.

questions.question: During endocytosis of a non-enveloped virus, what is formed inside the host cell?
questions.explanation: During endocytosis, an endosomal vesicle is formed inside the host cell.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Envelopes are not formed during entry.
Incorrect. Capsids are not formed during entry.
Correct. An endosomal vesicle forms.
Incorrect. Viruses do not have a nucleus.
questions.hint: What vesicle forms during endocytosis?

questions.question: How can enveloped viruses enter a host cell according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Enveloped viruses can enter by endocytosis or membrane fusion.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. They can also use membrane fusion.
Incorrect. They can also use endocytosis.
Incorrect. They do not use direct penetration.
Correct. Both endocytosis and membrane fusion are used.
questions.hint: They have two main entry mechanisms.

questions.question: In membrane fusion, what part of an enveloped virus is internalized into the host cell?
questions.explanation: In membrane fusion, the nucleocapsid is internalized into the host cell.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The envelope fuses with the membrane.
Incorrect. The spikes mediate fusion.
Correct. The nucleocapsid enters the cell.
Incorrect. The matrix protein is not the only part internalized.
questions.hint: What is the core structure that enters the cell?

questions.question: What is viral uncoating?
options: Separation of the viral genome from the outer viral structures
Attachment of the virus to the host receptor
Release of mature virions from the cell
questions.explanation: Viral uncoating is the separation of the viral genome from the outer viral structures.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This is assembly.
Correct. This is the definition of uncoating.
Incorrect. This is adsorption.
Incorrect. This is release.
questions.hint: The genome is released from the capsid.

questions.question: Where does the process of viral uncoating occur according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: Viral uncoating occurs in the cytoplasm.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. It occurs inside the cell.
Incorrect. It occurs in the cytoplasm, not only the nucleus.
Correct. Uncoating occurs in the cytoplasm.
Incorrect. The envelope is removed.
questions.hint: Where in the cell does uncoating take place?

questions.question: What happens to the infectivity of the internalized virus during uncoating?
options: It is abolished at this stage
It becomes independent of the host cell
questions.explanation: Infectivity is abolished at the uncoating stage.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Infectivity is lost.
Correct. The virus loses infectivity during uncoating.
Incorrect. It remains dependent on the host cell.
Incorrect. It does not change into bacteria.
questions.hint: The virus is no longer infectious as a complete particle.

questions.question: Where is the genome of most DNA viruses delivered after uncoating?
questions.explanation: The genome of most DNA viruses is delivered to the nucleus after uncoating.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Most DNA viruses go to the nucleus.
Incorrect. The plasma membrane is not the target.
Correct. Most DNA viruses replicate in the nucleus.
Incorrect. The Golgi is not the target.
questions.hint: Where does DNA replication occur in eukaryotes?

questions.question: Which DNA virus is the exception whose genome remains in the cytoplasm?
questions.explanation: Poxvirus is the exception whose genome remains in the cytoplasm.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Herpesvirus goes to the nucleus.
Correct. Poxvirus replicates in the cytoplasm.
Incorrect. Adenovirus goes to the nucleus.
Incorrect. Papillomavirus goes to the nucleus.
questions.hint: Which DNA virus is known for replicating in the cytoplasm?

questions.question: Where does the genome of most RNA viruses remain after uncoating?
questions.explanation: The genome of most RNA viruses remains in the cytoplasm after uncoating.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Most RNA viruses stay in the cytoplasm.
Correct. Most RNA viruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
Incorrect. The Golgi is not the primary site.
Incorrect. The genome remains inside the cell.
questions.hint: Where do most RNA viruses replicate?

questions.question: Which RNA virus group is the exception whose genome is delivered to the nucleus?
questions.explanation: Retroviruses are the exception whose genome is delivered to the nucleus.
optionExplanations: Correct. Retroviruses integrate into the host genome in the nucleus.
Incorrect. Picornaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
Incorrect. Coronaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
Incorrect. Rotaviruses replicate in the cytoplasm.
questions.hint: Which RNA virus needs to integrate into the host genome?

questions.question: What is the stage of viral replication in which viral macromolecules are synthesized called?
questions.explanation: The stage of viral replication in which viral macromolecules are synthesized is called the eclipse phase.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Adsorption is attachment.
Incorrect. Penetration is entry.
Correct. The eclipse phase is the synthesis stage.
Incorrect. Release is the final stage.
questions.hint: During this phase, no viral particles can be detected.

questions.question: Why is the synthesis stage called the eclipse phase?
options: Because the virus becomes visible under a microscope
Because no viral particles can be detected inside the infected host cell during this phase
Because the host cell immediately dies
Because the virus leaves the host cell
questions.explanation: It is called the eclipse phase because no viral particles can be detected inside the infected host cell during this phase.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. The virus is not visible.
Correct. No viral particles are detected.
Incorrect. The host cell does not immediately die.
Incorrect. The virus does not leave.
questions.hint: The virus seems to 'disappear' inside the cell.

questions.question: What occurs during the eclipse phase?
options: The viral genome is transcribed and translated into proteins required for viral macromolecule synthesis
The virus attaches to the host receptor
The mature virus buds from the cell
The viral envelope is destroyed outside the cell
questions.explanation: During the eclipse phase, the viral genome is transcribed and translated into proteins required for viral macromolecule synthesis.
optionExplanations: Correct. Viral macromolecules are synthesized.
Incorrect. Attachment occurs before the eclipse phase.
Incorrect. Budding occurs after the eclipse phase.
Incorrect. The envelope is not destroyed outside the cell.
questions.hint: What is being made during this phase?

questions.question: During the regulated gene expression cascade of DNA viruses, what is the primary functional class of viral products synthesized during the early transcription and translation phase?
options: Structural capsomeric proteins and envelope glycoprotein spikes required for virion morphogenesis.
Non-structural enzymes, regulatory proteins, and replication factors necessary for viral genome replication.
Fully assembled mature virions ready for immediate exocytic cellular egress.
Host cell ribosomal subunits and cytoplasmic eukaryotic initiation factors.
questions.explanation: Early transcription and translation yield non-structural viral proteins—such as viral polymerases, helicases, and transcriptional regulators—which alter host metabolic pathways and execute genomic replication prior to the expression of late structural proteins.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Structural capsomers and envelope glycoproteins are encoded during late gene expression following genome replication.
Correct. Early gene expression produces non-structural regulatory factors and enzymes (e.g., polymerases) required to initiate viral replication.
Incorrect. Morphogenesis into complete virions requires late structural proteins and occurs after genome replication is complete.
Incorrect. Ribosomal subunits and initiation factors are host cellular machinery, not viral early gene products.
questions.hint: Think about which proteins are logically required *first* to copy the viral genome versus those needed later to build the outer physical shell.

questions.question: Which of the following is an example of an early viral protein?
questions.explanation: Regulatory proteins are examples of early viral proteins.
optionExplanations: Correct. Regulatory proteins are early proteins.
Incorrect. Lipids are not proteins.
Incorrect. Ribosomes are host structures.
Incorrect. Capsids are late structural proteins.
questions.hint: Which of these is a non-structural protein made early?

questions.question: What is one major event occurring during late transcription and translation?
options: Initial attachment of the virus to the host cell
questions.explanation: Replication of the viral genome is a major event occurring during late transcription and translation.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Attachment occurs early.
Correct. Viral genome replication occurs during the late phase.
Incorrect. Host receptors are not destroyed.
Incorrect. Adsorption occurs early.
questions.hint: What major biosynthetic process happens in the late phase?

questions.question: In the temporally regulated replication cycle of DNA viruses, which functional class of viral proteins is predominantly translated during the late stage following genomic replication?
options: Non-structural regulatory proteins, such as viral DNA polymerases and early transcriptional activators.
Structural proteins constituting capsomers, envelope glycoproteins, and virion assembly factors.
Host cell extracellular matrix proteins required for membrane fluidity.
Cellular ribosomal RNA molecules and nuclear histones.
questions.explanation: Viral gene expression is temporally orchestrated into early and late phases. The early phase encodes non-structural enzymes required for viral genome replication (such as DNA polymerases), whereas the late phase (occurring post-genome replication) encodes structural viral proteins (e.g., capsid proteins, envelope glycoproteins) needed for assembling progeny virions.
questions.subtopic: Viral Replication Cycle and Gene Expression
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Non-structural enzymes (like DNA polymerases) are translated during the early phase to prepare for viral genome replication.
Correct. Late-stage transcription and translation focus on synthesizing structural proteins and assembly factors needed to build new virions.
Incorrect. Viruses shut down host translation and do not encode or upregulate host extracellular matrix proteins.
Incorrect. Ribosomal RNAs and histones are host cellular products, not viral proteins synthesized during late translation.
questions.hint: Distinguish between non-structural enzymatic proteins needed *before* replication (early) versus structural proteins needed for virion morphogenesis *after* replication (late).

questions.question: What is another term for viral assembly?
questions.explanation: Viral maturation is another term for viral assembly.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Adsorption is attachment.
Correct. Maturation is another term for assembly.
Incorrect. Tropism is tissue specificity.
Incorrect. Penetration is entry.
questions.hint: It is the stage where components come together.

questions.question: What happens during viral assembly?
options: All synthesized viral components irreversibly combine to form mature viral particles
All synthesized viral components reversibly combine to form mature viral particles
The host cell produces bacterial particles
questions.explanation: During viral assembly, all synthesized viral components irreversibly combine to form mature viral particles.
optionExplanations: Correct. Components combine to form virions.
Incorrect. It binds eternally.
Incorrect. The genome is packaged, not destroyed.
Incorrect. Host cells do not produce bacteria.
questions.hint: What is being formed during assembly?

questions.question: What does functional viral packaging mean?
options: Enclosing the complete viral genome inside its capsid
Removing the viral genome from the capsid
Replacing the viral genome with host DNA
questions.explanation: Functional viral packaging means enclosing the complete viral genome inside its capsid.
optionExplanations: Correct. The complete genome is packaged.
Incorrect. The genome is enclosed, not removed.
Incorrect. Host DNA is not used.
Incorrect. The envelope is not removed.
questions.hint: What is the goal of packaging?

questions.question: Which set of aberrant physical structures typically arises when aberrant or non-functional viral packaging occurs during assembly?
options: Fully infectious, wild-type progeny virions with enhanced replication kinetics.
Defective interfering particles, pseudoviruses, and empty capsid shells lacking genomic core nucleic acid.
questions.explanation: Non-functional or aberrant packaging during virion assembly leads to assembly errors such as empty capsid shells (coreless capsids), defective interfering particles containing truncated/damaged genomes, or pseudoviruses (capsids encapsidating host cellular nucleic acids or foreign viral genomes instead of the complete viral genome).
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Aberrant or defective packaging compromises viral infectivity and replication kinetics rather than producing wild-type, highly infectious particles.
Incorrect. Helper viruses are fully functional intact viruses required to complement replication-defective strains, not defective assembly by-products.
Correct. Errors in genome packaging yield defective interfering particles, pseudoviruses, and genome-free empty capsids (coreless virions).
Incorrect. Bacterial spheroplasts are cell-wall-deficient prokaryotes, completely unrelated to eukaryotic viral capsid assembly errors.
questions.hint: Consider the structural and genomic defects that occur when a protein shell fails to correctly encapsidate its intended viral nucleic acid genome.

questions.question: What is a complete virus?
options: A virus containing only host chromosome material
A fully mature virus containing a complete viral genome and capsid, with or without an envelope
A virus containing an incomplete viral genome
questions.explanation: A complete virus is a fully mature virus containing a complete viral genome and capsid, with or without an envelope.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes a coreless virus.
Incorrect. This describes a pseudovirus.
Correct. This is the definition of a complete virus.
Incorrect. This describes a defective virus.
questions.hint: It has all necessary components.

questions.question: What characterizes a defective virus?
options: It contains only host chromosome material
It contains a complete viral genome and always replicates independently
It contains an incomplete viral genome and cannot replicate without a helper virus
questions.explanation: A defective virus contains an incomplete viral genome and cannot replicate without a helper virus.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. This describes a coreless virus.
Incorrect. This describes a pseudovirus.
Incorrect. Defective viruses cannot replicate independently.
Correct. This is the definition of a defective virus.
questions.hint: It needs help to replicate.

questions.question: Which virus was given as an example of a defective virus?
questions.explanation: Hepatitis D virus is an example of a defective virus.
optionExplanations: Correct. Hepatitis D is a defective virus.

questions.question: What is the process by which a defective virus is formed called?
questions.explanation: Premature capsid inclusion is the process by which a defective virus is formed.
optionExplanations: Incorrect. Capsid mispackaging forms pseudoviruses.
Incorrect. Budding is a release mechanism.
Correct. Premature capsid inclusion forms defective viruses.
Incorrect. Membrane fusion is an entry mechanism.

Part of the host chromosome instead of viral nucleic acid, enclosed by a capsid with or without an envelope

questions.question: Why can a pseudovirus not replicate even in the presence of a helper virus?

It cannot enter a host cell

questions.question: What is the process by which a pseudovirus is formed called?
questions.explanation: Capsid mispackaging is the process by which a pseudovirus is formed.

questions.question: What is the ability of a coreless virus to infect or replicate?

It can infect but cannot replicate
It can replicate but cannot infect

questions.question: What is the last step of the viral replication cycle?
